title: The Epic and the Unoccupied Garden
summary: A peace negotiator’s protected zone, a founding ruler’s evolving epic, and a naval trade reversal converge in a disputed upland valley.
source_notes: A peace process and a withdrawn-force negotiating zone become a protected garden whose practical dependencies remain contested.
A founding ruler preserved through oral epic and later corroborating records becomes layered memory rather than literal reproduction of a real epic.
A naval victory redirecting established trade becomes a downstream battle affecting sponsors; modern naval technology is excluded.
A fertile region divided among competing powers becomes overlapping claims whose residents’ needs exceed the positions of outside rulers.

entries.title: Pastren of the Meeting Garden
entries.body:
Pastren withdrew officers to create negotiating space but left uncertain who would inspect armed visitors. His hope was genuine and incomplete. Later accounts must preserve both, because the zone’s failures arose partly from practical terms its ideal language omitted.

Later accounts make Pastren of the Meeting Garden the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Epic and the Unoccupied Garden. An upland founder’s life survived through performed epic alongside sparse independent records. Later households used the epic to justify incompatible claims to a fertile valley. In 779 a negotiator established a garden zone from which armed officers withdrew for talks, hoping protected meeting space would end recurring conflict. Outside coalitions continued contesting its borders and access. A naval battle far downstream redirected trade, weakening sponsors who had supplied the negotiations and strengthening new patrons. The peace zone became both a genuine refuge and a place where rivals accumulated influence. Present gardeners compare heroic memory, signed terms, and changed supply routes to preserve talks without pretending withdrawal of one force made the valley free of coercion.

In the connected record, [The Unoccupied Garden](b039-the-unoccupied-garden.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Resident Within Neutrality](b039-the-resident-within-neutrality.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether the meeting garden can remain protected when the trade revenues supporting its food and repairs now pass through rival downstream hands.

entries.title: The Unoccupied Garden
entries.body:
The garden contains cultivated paths and pomegranate shade rather than empty neutral ground. Local households maintain it. Calling it unoccupied concealed their work and claims, making a peace image dependent on people the negotiations initially treated as scenery.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Valley Epic Keepers
entries.body:
Keepers perform variant lives of the founder and identify their teaching lineages. Outside claimants want one fixed version supporting exclusive title. The group preserves variation beside corroborating records, refusing to make a meaningful epic an automatic cadastral map.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Downstream Fleet Reversal
entries.body:
A coalition fleet lost control of a key harbor and trade shifted toward victors’ landings. Valley sponsors lost revenue before negotiators revised budgets. The peace garden’s shortages therefore originated far beyond the speeches and patrols visible within its borders.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Founder’s Unverified Saddle
entries.body:
The saddle is old and repeatedly repaired, but no custody chain links it securely to the epic ruler. Keepers label the uncertainty. Its teaching use remains valuable without demanding that every cherished object authenticate the most prestigious possible owner.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Variant Spoken First
entries.body:
Performers identify which epic version they will use before reciting. Listeners can compare without interrupting every line. The custom protects art’s continuity while preventing a chosen variant from silently presenting itself as the only history ever remembered.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Founder Beyond the Epic
entries.body:
The booklet compares oral episodes with independent travel and tribute records. Some details align and others remain unconfirmed. Readers preserve that pattern, allowing historical existence to be established without requiring every dramatic event to become literal fact.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Garden Border Hoopoe
entries.body:
Hoopoes nest across political boundary markers and feed in cultivated beds. Patrols clear vegetation to improve sightlines. Gardeners negotiate narrow inspection paths, preserving habitat and crops while addressing real safety needs without stripping the whole meeting place bare.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Negotiators’ Food Road
entries.body:
The road connects kitchens to talks through several disputed jurisdictions. Each claims inspection rights. Finite passage agreements keep food moving, showing that a protected meeting depends on many modest commitments outside the apparently neutral room.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Resident Within Neutrality
entries.body:
A peace zone must recognize residents’ cultivation and custody even when armed authorities withdraw. The clause prevents neutral language from erasing ordinary land relations. It protects useful talks without pretending hosts surrendered every right by welcoming them.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The First Withdrawal Ceremony
entries.body:
Officers left amid public applause, but visitors continued arriving armed under different credentials. The ceremony achieved a real reduction in one force. Inspection records reveal why that achievement could not substitute for the broader access rules the garden still needed.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Peace Table Grain Cup
entries.body:
The cup measures food supplied per delegate and exposes expensive entourages. Patrons call counting inhospitable. Hosts explain that accounting makes continued welcome possible, preventing a prestigious meeting from exhausting the households whose generosity sustains it.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Epic’s Unchosen Listener
entries.body:
Listeners may decline a version without losing access to garden meals. Claimant rulers object that refusal insults ancestral authority. The practice keeps performance from manufacturing consent, especially where an epic is being used to support disputed title.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Naval Toll’s Inland Costs
entries.body:
The account follows increased harbor fees through transport, kitchens, and negotiating budgets. It documents concrete effects without claiming the battle explains every valley conflict. Trade change becomes one important dependency among several, not a universal historical cause.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Founder’s Empty Reins
entries.body:
Stored reins tighten briefly near a basin when promised host provisions fail. Leather contraction explains ordinary tension. The unresolved recurrence remains limited to the hosting pledge, preventing an evocative relic from deciding every claimant’s version of the founder’s will.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Peace Garden Cultivation
entries.body:
Gardeners schedule harvest around talks while reserving time for pruning and channel work. Sponsors fund impressive meeting tents more readily. Public accounts make maintenance visible, keeping peace’s setting alive rather than sacrificing cultivation to its ceremonial image.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Garden’s New Sponsor
entries.body:
A victorious downstream house offers food in exchange for privileged access. Hosts fear losing talks if they refuse. Negotiators seek several bounded contributions, reducing dependence on one patron without pretending the garden can feed everyone through neutrality alone.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
